context_blurb:
A dead animal left out in summer soon crawls with maggots. For some two thousand years, most learned people thought the rotting flesh itself made them. In 1668 the Italian doctor Francesco Redi published experiments that tested it with nothing but flasks, paper, string and gauze.

The old belief was spontaneous generation, the idea that living things can spring from lifeless matter with no parents. In ancient Greece, Aristotle wrote that eels and certain insects come from mud and decaying matter. In the 1600s the Flemish chemist van Helmont even gave a recipe for mice: wheat grains and a dirty shirt, left in a pot for three weeks. The wheat and the shirt simply gave mice food and a place to hide. The opposite idea, that life comes only from life, is called biogenesis.

Redi, chief doctor to the Medici rulers of Tuscany, watched snakes, fish and meat rot one summer. Each time, before a single maggot showed, flies had landed on the flesh, always of the kinds that later hatched. He saw maggots turn into hard, egg-shaped cases, now called pupae, from which flies of those same kinds broke out. He also found eggs on meat and fish like the clusters flies leave there. So he began to suspect that maggots are young flies, hatched from eggs that flies leave behind.

In July he filled four wide-mouthed flasks with a piece of veal, a snake, some river fish and four little eels from the river Arno, one to a flask. He sealed each mouth tightly with paper and string. Four more flasks got the same things but stayed open. Soon the open flasks swarmed with maggots, as flies came and went freely. In the sealed ones he never saw a maggot, though months passed. Now and then a maggot was found outside, at a flask's lip, as if trying to get in.

The open flasks held the same meats in the same weeks, so the covering was the only difference, and their swarms were a check that this meat, that summer, could breed maggots. Without that check, a critic could say the sealed flasks would have stayed empty anyway.

Redi saw a second objection coming. Paper and string shut out the air as well as the flies, so a critic could say the meat had bred no maggots only because it lacked fresh air. Nor had the sealed meat simply stayed fresh: the fish broke down into a cloudy liquid and the veal slowly dried hard, yet no maggot appeared.

So Redi let the air in and kept the flies out. He put fish and meat in a much bigger vessel, where air could move freely, and stretched a very fine Naples gauze over the top. Drawn by the smell, flies buzzed round it and landed on the gauze, and some left maggots there, but on the meat and fish no maggot ever appeared. Air reached the meat but flies did not, so the maggots came from flies, not from meat or air.

The German Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher had written that dead flies, steeped in honeyed water and warmed over hot ashes, breed tiny worms that sprout wings. Redi replied that the sweet water had a single job: it drew living flies to the dead ones, and those flies left their young on the bodies. In his own trial, dead flies shut in a sealed vessel bred nothing, while maggots appeared among dead flies in an open one.

Still the argument did not end. Through the new microscopes, naturalists saw tiny living things crowding drops of water and broths, and some held that these sprang up on their own. Redi had watched only for maggots and flies, which anyone can see, so his flasks said nothing about life too small for the eye. His results stood; they simply never tested the tiny life.

In the 1740s John Needham, an English priest skilled with the microscope, briefly boiled mutton broth and sealed it. Days later it teemed with tiny life. Needham believed the boiling had killed every living thing in the broth, so to him the new life must have arisen there by a life force of its own. Later the Italian priest Lazzaro Spallanzani boiled broths an hour or more and melted the flask necks shut, and nothing grew. Needham's short boil had most likely left some tiny life alive. Louis Pasteur's flasks ended the old idea in the 1860s.
